59419-the-journal-of-geology-may-june-18:
The Journal of Geology for May and June 1893 is one issue of a semi-quarterly magazine for earth science. Its lead paper treats the typical Laurentian area of Canada. Logan gave the name Laurentian in 1854 to the rocks of the Laurentian Mountains north of the Saint Lawrence. The paper confines itself to that first-studied district, near Quebec and Ontario.

Other papers describe basalt rocks from southern Texas and the Baraboo quartzite ranges of central Wisconsin. The chemical relation of iron and manganese in sedimentary rocks gets a study. Rivers of Connecticut and the history of the Laurentian basin follow. Editorials, reviews, and abstracts of current writing close a dense, learned number.
britannica-1911-arezzo:
Arezzo is a town and bishop seat in Tuscany, Italy, south east of Florence. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the capital of Arezzo province and stands on a hill slope. Rich farm land surrounds the town in its fertile district near by.

Walls built in thirteen twenty ring the town, later rebuilt by Cosimo de Medici. A fort at the top was built in fifteen o two and later undone. The Gothic cathedral was begun in twelve seventy seven and holds fine sculpture. Its high altar holds the tomb of Saint Donatus, patron of Arezzo. Glass windows and clay relief work add more art to its rooms.
britannica-1911-azo:
Azo (c. 1150-1230) was an Italian jurist born at Bologna, pupil of Joannes Bassianus and later professor of civil law at Bologna's university. The entry first separates him from two later Bologna canon lawyers of the same name, Azo Lambertaccius and Azo de Ramenghis, to keep the records straight.

Azo ranked high among the glossators, the scholars who explained Roman law in notes. His Readings on the Code were gathered by a pupil and completed by others. They gave a methodical account of Roman law. Their weight in court was such that a saying ran: who has not Azzo does not go to court. He also took part in Bologna's city life after its winning of self-rule. Accursius was among his pupils.
britannica-1911-bartolini-lorenzo:
Lorenzo Bartolini (1777–1850), an Italian sculptor born at Vernio in Tuscany, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. He first built skill and a name as a modeller in alabaster, then went to Paris in 1797 to study painting and afterwards sculpture. His bas-relief Cleobis and Biton won the Academy's second prize in 1803. It fixed his fame as a sculptor at once and brought him patrons with influence in the Paris art world.

Napoleon became Bartolini's great patron. For him the sculptor made a colossal bust, and Napoleon then sent him to Carrara to found a school of sculpture. After Napoleon's fall he settled in Florence for the rest of his life. His many works include a great number of busts, plus the group of Charity, Hercules and Lichas, and Faith in God. Italian opinion, the entry says, links his qualities with those of Thorwaldsen and Canova.
britannica-1911-bellini-lorenzo:
Lorenzo Bellini (1643–1704) was an Italian physician and anatomist born at Florence. At twenty he had already studied the build of the kidneys and described the small ducts that still carry his name. Pisa made him professor of theoretical medicine, then moved him to the chair of anatomy.

Bellini spent thirty years at Pisa before Florence called him home as doctor to the grand duke Cosimo III. He also served Pope Clement XI as senior consulting physician. His collected works came out at Venice in 1708, four years after his death at Florence. The entry is a compact record of a young researcher’s find and a long, honoured career at two courts.
britannica-1911-bellini-vincenzo:
Vincenzo Bellini (1801–1835) was an Italian opera composer born at Catania in Sicily. Music ran in his family: father and grandfather were both composers of some standing. Trained at home first, he went to the Naples conservatoire to study singing and composition under Tritto and Zingarelli.

Bellini’s first opera appeared in 1825, and Il Pirata of 1827, written for La Scala with his friend Felice Romano, made his name across Europe. New operas followed almost yearly, sung by great voices and received with rapture in France, Italy, Germany and England. Wagner later praised the simple, noble melody Bellini restored to him when German orchestral writing had worn him out.
britannica-1911-bernini-giovanni-lorenzo:
Giovanni Lorenzo Bernini (1598–1680) was an Italian artist born at Naples. He won fame first as a sculptor and architect, less as a painter. His early skill in modelling brought him court favour at Rome. Pope Urban VIII, once Maffeo Barberini, became his special patron. Bernini designed that pope's palace. His first sculpted group, Apollo and Daphne, set a mark later groups never matched.

The 1911 Britannica entry notes the demand for his portrait busts. Charles I of England sent him three portraits by Van Dyck to work from. His designs for St Peter's great colonnade brought him perhaps his widest fame. Louis XIV summoned him to Paris over the Louvre, then set his designs aside. He died leaving a fortune over £100,000.
britannica-1911-brizo:
Brizo was an ancient goddess worshipped on the island of Delos. Her gift was prophecy through dreams: people who consulted her about fishing and seafaring received oracles while they slept. That tie to the risks of the sea shapes every line of the short entry.

Women of Delos made her offerings meant to win her protection for those engaged on the sea. The gifts were curious: little boats filled with all kinds of eatables, but with one strict rule, no fish among them. The source named for the custom is Athenaeus. A dream oracle, an island shrine and boat-shaped offerings without fish make up the whole of this compact notice on a minor sea goddess.
britannica-1911-camuccini-vincenzo:
Vincenzo Camuccini lived from 1773 to 1844 and was an Italian painter of history. The 1911 Britannica life opens at Rome, where he was born and raised. His brother Pietro, a restorer of pictures, gave him his schooling in art. An engraver named Borubelli also taught the young painter his craft. Till age thirty he did no more than copy the great masters.

Raphael was his chief study in those long years of training. As an artist in his own right he followed David of France. His works show great cleverness and patient care, not fresh genius. That verdict in the entry is frank, if a touch harsh in tone. Fame and honours still rained on him from courts across Italy.
britannica-1911-civerchio-vincenzo:
Civerchio, Vincenzo was an early 16th century Italian painter, born at Crema, and the entry gathers his works town by town. Altar-pieces by him stand at Brescia, in the entry's first notice. At Crema itself the altar-piece at the duomo dates from 1509 and anchors his home record. His Birth of Christ hangs in the Brera at Milan, a named work in a major gallery.

Other works by Civerchio are at Lovere, a smaller place named without detail. Two of those Lovere works date from 1539 and 1540, late in the span the entry covers. No training, patrons or style are discussed, and no death date is given. Brescia, Crema, Milan and Lovere, with three dates, form the whole factual frame offered for this painter.
britannica-1911-ezzo:
Ezzo, also called Ehrenfried, a count palatine in Lorraine who lived from about 954 to 1024, has a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Hermann, a count palatine with lands near Bonn. His marriage to Matilda, a daughter of the emperor Otto the Second, brought him to the front. Her lands in Thuringia and Franconia added much to his power.

Under Otto the Third, his brother in law, Ezzo rose high, and his rank was made one that passed to his heirs. Henry the Second was less warm to him, and there was strife in 1011. Peace was bought with a gift of lands, and good terms held from then on. Ezzo died at Saalfeld in 1024 and was laid to rest at Brauweiler, a house of monks that he had founded.
britannica-1911-gioberti-vincenzo:
Gioberti, Vincenzo, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an Italian thinker. Born in Turin on the 5th of April 1801, he trained for the priesthood. He was ordained in 1825 and at first lived a quiet, retired life. In time the fate of Italy and new thought drew him in more.

The freedom of Italy became the ruling aim of his whole life. He sought it free from foreign masters and foreign modes of thought. In his mind Italy's old weight in Europe was bound to papal rule. Yet he meant a rule of mind, not of arms or state power. The king made him a court chaplain in his rise. In 1833 court foes had him jailed and then exiled with no trial.
britannica-1911-gozo:
Gozo is an island of the Maltese group in the Mediterranean Sea, second in size to Malta. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its shape and size in brief: an oval isle lying north west of Malta, with an area of about twenty five square miles. Its chief town stands near the middle of the island, on one of a cluster of steep cone shaped hills.

The entry adds the town count from the census of the day and the isle count a few years on. It notes the port bay on the south east shore, below a fort, and says the land and look of Gozo match those of Malta. Readers get a short, clear sketch of the island as it stood at that date.
britannica-1911-gozzoli-benozzo:
Benozzo Gozzoli was an Italian painter born in Florence in 1420 or 1424. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows him first as a helper of Fra Angelico. He followed that master to Rome and worked with him at Orvieto. In 1449 he left Angelico and went to Montefalco in Umbria. There he painted a Madonna and Child with saints and angels. An altar piece of Saint Thomas shows his early debt to Angelico.

In the friary at Montefalco he filled a choir with scenes from the life of Saint Francis. Heads of Dante, Petrarch, and Giotto stand among its figures. That work, done in 1452, mixes Angelico's manner with Giotto's. After stays at Perugia he returned to his native Florence. By the end of 1459 he had near finished his great work there. It is the Journey of the Magi in the Riccardi palace chapel.
britannica-1911-gravina-giovanni-vincenz:
Giovanni Vincenzo Gravina (1664-1718) was an Italian writer and legal scholar from Calabria. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his training under his uncle Gregorio Caloprese. He studied civil and canon law at Naples in his youth. At Rome in 1695 he helped found the Academy of Arcadians.

A split in that academy in 1711 led him to form a rival group. He refused church honors that the pope offered him more than once. Chairs in civil law and then canon law at La Sapienza followed. His main works treat the origins of civil law in three volumes. He was also adoptive father to the poet Metastasio.
britannica-1911-hanna-marcus-alonzo:
Marcus Alonzo Hanna (1837–1904) was an American politician. He was born in Ohio on 24 September 1837. Cleveland received the family in 1852. His father ran a wholesale grocery business there. Hanna joined that business and left college early. In 1867 he partnered with his father-in-law in coal and iron. M. A. Hanna & Company dates from 1877. Lake steamships and mines extended the firm's reach.

Politics claimed him seriously only after 1880. In 1896 he managed McKinley's nomination canvass personally. The St Louis convention gave McKinley the prize. Hanna then chaired the Republican National Committee. He ran the 1896 campaign against Bryan with consummate skill. Ohio sent him to the Senate in 1897. Conservatives later saw him as a possible president for 1904. He died at Washington on 15 February 1904.
britannica-1911-hervas-y-panduro-lorenzo:
Lorenzo Hervás y Panduro (1735–1809) was a Spanish philologist, born at Horcajo in Cuenca on the 10th of May 1735. He joined the Jesuits in 1745 and in time taught philosophy and humanities at Madrid and Murcia. When the Jesuit order was banished from Spain in 1767, he settled at Forli in Italy. There he wrote his Idea dell' Universo, which ran to 22 volumes (1778–1792).

Hervás returned to Spain in 1798 and published his famous Catálogo de las lenguas de las naciones conocidas in six volumes (1800–1805). In it he gathered the traits of three hundred languages and drew up grammars of forty. In 1802 he became librarian of the Quirinal Palace in Rome, where he died on the 24th of August 1809. Max Müller credits him with getting ahead of Humboldt, and with a brilliant find: he fixed the kinship between the Malay and Polynesian families of speech.
britannica-1911-lotto-lorenzo:
Lotto, Lorenzo is an art life story from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an Italian painter of the Renaissance. Lorenzo Lotto was born near 1480, most likely at Venice, and died in 1556. For years his birthplace was put at Bergamo, Venice, or Treviso. A paper found by Dr Bampo settled the point in favour of Venice, and his will points to 1480 as the year.

The article says Lotto long stood in the shade of Titian, Giorgione, and Palma, three great men of his own age. Art writers thus passed him by until Bernhard Berenson wrote a study that set him back in his right place. Old accounts made him a pupil of Bellini, of Previtali, or even of Leonardo. Berenson showed that his true master was Alvise Vivarini, whose stern faith marked the young painter's work.
britannica-1911-mascheroni-lorenzo:
Lorenzo Mascheroni is the subject of a short life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He lived from 1750 to 1800 and was an Italian worker in geometry. He held the chair of maths at the town of Pavia and wrote a range of works in that field.

The article centres on his best known book, printed at Pavia in 1797. Its title means the geometry of the compass. Inside, each task is solved with the circle alone, with no straight edge used. The text calls many of the solutions most clever. Some are said to hold real use in practice. A French version came out at Paris in 1798. That same version carried a life of the author by its translator.
britannica-1911-parenzo:
Parenzo is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a seaport of Austria. It lies in Istria, far south of Trieste by rail. A count from 1900 gives it 9962 people, mostly Italian. It stands on the west coast of Istria. The town is built on a peninsula of low land. No part stands more than five feet above the sea. Roman pavements lie three feet below the present surface. From that fact, scholars infer the coast is slowly sinking.

The town holds great historic and architectural interest. Its cathedral of Saint Maurus is well preserved. It was erected probably between 535 and 543. The basilican type of the church is very pure. It has three naves and a six sided apse. The church proper is only 120 feet long. A square atrium with arches stands before its west door. A now roofless baptistery stands west of that atrium.
britannica-1911-saluzzo:
Saluzzo is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a city in Italy. It is a city and episcopal see of Piedmont. It lies in the province of Cuneo, south of Turin. It stands near thirteen hundred feet above the sea. A count from 1901 gives the town 10,306 people. The upper town keeps part of its old fortifications. Those walls guarded it before the plague of 1630. The city once held upwards of thirty thousand people.

The old castle of the marquises now serves as a prison. The Gothic cathedral was built from 1480 to 1511. Tombs of the marquises stand inside that church. Two other churches and a museum draw notice in the text. Railways and steam tramways link the city outward. The castle of Manta near by holds frescoes of note. Those wall paintings date from the fifteenth century. The line of the marquises began in 1142.
britannica-1911-tagliacozzo:
Tagliacozzo is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a town of the Abruzzi in Italy, in the province of Aquila, east of Rome by rail. Population figures for town and commune in nineteen hundred one are both given. It lies high above sea level at the mouth of a deep ravine.

Old churches stand in the town, one noted for a fine rose window in its front. Medieval houses and a palace built by the Orsini in the late thirteen hundreds are also described. At the end of twelve sixty eight a battle was fought there. Conradin was defeated by Charles of Anjou in that fight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andreas-pozzo:
Andreas Pozzo, called Puteus, was an Italian painter and architect of the Baroque period, born at Trent in 1642 and died at Vienna in 1709. Most of his life passed in Genoa, Rome, Turin, and Vienna. After literary studies he gave himself to painting, and at twenty-four he entered the Society of Jesus as a lay brother. A memoir and a medal marked his memory after his death.

Pozzo had no rival as a master of perspective, creating illusion with light, colour, and architectural background. Baroque painting then covered domes, ceilings, and vaultings, and Pozzo mastered this new style. At Rome, his San Ignazio frescoes on ceiling, dome, and apse win great admiration. His manual, Perspectiva pictorum et architectorum, published at Rome in 1693 and 1700, gives full instruction in his method and directions for church furniture. His decorative work suited the taste of the period and the pomp of religious services.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arezzo:
Arezzo is a diocese of Tuscany in Italy, directly dependent on the Holy See, with forty towns in Arezzo province, ten in Siena, and one in Perugia. It counts 250,000 Catholics, 330 parishes, 563 diocesan priests, 149 regulars, 145 seminarians, and 436 churches or chapels. Its bishops' list runs fairly regularly from AD 250. Arezzo is very ancient and among the first Italian cities to receive the gospel, by tradition from Romulus, later bishop of Fiesole and a disciple of Paul.

It grew into a bishopric about 304 under Satyrus, whose successor Donatus is patron of St. Peter the Apostle's cathedral, and its first eight bishops were saints. Clement XII, when his nephew Cardinal Guadagni was bishop, granted Arezzo in perpetuity archiepiscopal insignia, the pallium and double cross. Its cathedral is an imposing thirteenth-century Gothic building, while Santa Maria of the ninth century is called the old parish church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caiazzo:
Caiazzo stands in the province of Caserta, Italy, among the Tifati mountains near the Volturno, and in Roman times was called Calatia, of note in the Samnite wars and Hannibal's wars. Legend credits Saint Priscus, first Bishop of Capua, with bringing Christianity there. Its first known bishop, Arigisus, cannot predate the Lombard settlement of the early seventh century.

Later bishops include Jacopo, exiled by Frederick II for loyalty to the Holy See, and Giuliano Frangipane, elected in 1472. Fabio Mirto sat at Trent and died as nuncio to Paris in 1587. The diocese holds 25,000 people in 72 churches and chapels, served by 35 secular priests, with 3 religious institutes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calabozo:
Calabozo is a town in Venezuela on the Guárico River, 120 miles south-southwest of Caracas, founded as a town in 1730 by the Guipuzcoa Company on the site of an Indian village. It stands on low ground, flooded in the rainy season, with thermal springs nearby, a college and public schools, and a fair trade, chiefly in cattle.

Pius IX created the Diocese of Calabozo on 7 March 1863, and its first bishop was consecrated on 30 October 1881. The diocese covers part of Guárico with portions of Apure, Zamora, Portuguesa, Cojedes, and Guzman Blanco, counting 310,000 Catholics, 38 priests, and 70 churches and chapels. Calabozo answers to Caracas as suffragan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ezzo:
Ezzo, a Bamberg priest of the eleventh century, wrote a famed poem, the Song of the Miracles of Christ, also called the Anegenge, or Beginning. Barack found it in an eleventh-century Strasburg manuscript, but only a few strophes there. The full song runs to thirty-four strophes in the later Vorau manuscript. The Life of Altmann tells that in 1065, when rumors of the world's end ran rife, many set out for Jerusalem under Bishop Gunther.

Ezzo wrote the poem for that pilgrimage, though the Vorau opening says simply that the bishop ordered him to write the song. Its effect, we are told, was such that all hastened to take monastic vows. The poem uses the East Franconian dialect. In earnest language it tells the Creation, the Fall, and the Redemption of mankind. Piper edited it, and Steinmayer edited it again in a Berlin collection of 1892.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gozo:
Gozo is a diocese comprising the island of Gozo in the Mediterranean, seventeen miles west of Valletta harbour in Malta, with the islet of Comino, and a population of 22,700 souls. More picturesque than Malta, it is famed for the grotto of Calypso and the ruins of a Cyclopean temple nearby. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a diocese born of the clergy's and people's repeated prayer.

Until 1864 Gozo belonged to the Diocese of Malta. Pius IX erected it as a separate diocese immediately subject to the Holy See. Francesco Michele Butigieg, consecrated at Rome in 1863, became its first bishop in September 1864 and entered his cathedral the next month. Through Pietro Pace a diocesan seminary rose on the old San Giuliano Hospital site in 1866, placed under the Jesuits at Pius IX's express desire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guido-of-arez:
Guido of Arezzo, a Benedictine monk born near Paris about 995, gave Western music the staff notation still in use. Troubled by the confusion in teaching liturgical chant, he devised a clearer method at Pomposa and Arezzo. Pope John XIX summoned him to Rome after learning how easily the new notation let a singer read melodies without a master.

Before Guido, neumes, or nodding signs, showed rhythm only roughly, and intervals had to be guessed from memory or from a master's voice. He built on two coloured lines for F and C, adding two more lines and using the spaces between them. Joining letters to neume signs, he let both pitch steps and rhythm be read at sight. Four lines served the range of Gregorian chant, and the F and C letters later became clefs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-molfetta-terl:
Molfetta, Terlizzi and Giovinazzo form a group of united dioceses on Italy's Adriatic coast in Apulia, and this entry sketches each town's past and present church life. Molfetta's site was settled in prehistoric times, its cathedral stands in the town, and a nearby shrine of the Virgin of the Martyrs holds an image Crusaders brought in 1188.

Its first recorded bishop, John, dates to 1136, and the see passed from Bari's oversight to direct dependence on Rome in 1484. Giovinazzo, possibly the ancient Egnatia, has held a bishop since 1071, while Terlizzi became a see in 1731 to settle disputes over its standing. The entry closes with parish and clergy counts for all three, totalling tens of thousands of Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saluzzo:
Saluzzo, a diocese in Cuneo province in Piedmont, stands on a hill above a wide, well-farmed plain, with iron, lead, silver, marble, and slate in the nearby mountains. Its cathedral, built between 1480 and 1511 in half-Gothic style, holds a fine high altar and rich sculpture. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia tours churches, tombs, and civic buildings.

St Bernard's church keeps tombs of the della Torre counts. St Dominic's holds the tomb of Marquess Lodovico II and his wife from 1504, with the chapel of the Holy Sepulchre. The old town hall of 1462, with its bold tower, now serves the assizes. Birthplace of Silvio Pellico, the printer Bodoni, Abate Denina, and the anatomist Malcarne, Saluzzo began as a town of the mountain Ligurians before Rome, under Consul Fulvius, brought it under control.
doe-osti-3362959-detecting-and-character:
Yingcai Zheng of the University of Houston and Lianjie Huang of Los Alamos National Laboratory report under award DE-EE0008764 on finding cracks with artificial intelligence, with Cyrq Energy staff sharing the work. Geothermal wells need fracture zones, since hot water moves through cracks, not solid rock. The project serves the Geothermal Technologies Office goals on exploration and on data and modeling. Its tool is a convolutional neural network, an image-reading model, turned on seismic pictures of the ground.

Field work centered on Soda Lake and Carson Sink in Nevada. Gravity and 2D seismic lines show Carson Sink as a stretched basin of raised and dropped blocks, where the raised block edges form ramps that often end transfer zones. At Soda Lake, depth slices show northwest to southeast faults, and the team proposed well sites from the mapped patterns.
podcast-joerogan-MXuwPUqSczo:
Philosopher Andy Norman joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1653 to argue that minds need immune systems. Norman studies how bad ideas spread like infections, and how people can learn to spot them before they take hold. His term for the gaps in that defense gives the talk its hook.

He explains mental immunity in plain terms: the habits of asking for evidence, hearing the other side, and slowing down outrage. Rogan tests the idea against conspiracy culture, including his own audience. The episode is a practical talk on thinking clearly in a loud age, from a teacher who treats doubt as a skill.
